source.title: Trojan activation attack: Red-teaming large language models using activation steering for safety-alignment

record.file_problem: not stated; the provided text is a full paper.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests task-specific activation steering attacks, not the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction or any of the listed claim versions. It does report refusal outcomes after steering, recorded below as related findings that fit none of the versions.
record.gate_note: The steering vectors are averages of activation differences between a target model's aligned output and a teacher model's output, selected for a target alignment and added at a selected layer. The paper does not test the specified refusal direction, remove it, or measure its effect on general capability. Refusal results under this different attack are recorded as fits_no_version. Truthfulness, toxicity, and sentiment outcomes are omitted because they do not measure a behavior named by the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper never builds or tests the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. TA2's vector is the mean activation difference between a target model and a non-aligned teacher model on the same prompts, at a searched layer and strength. It is applied as an inference-time attack on toxicity, bias, harmfulness and truthfulness. It does not ablate a refusal direction, induce refusal on harmless prompts, check general capability, or edit weights. The paper predates the original source and does not cite it. Its refusal-rate changes concern a related but different construct, so they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, with two qualifications. Scaling across model sizes (7B/13B/70B) was shown only on TruthfulQA (Table 9); all refusal results are 7B. The authors also note that steered AdvBench outputs, though not refused, may lack practical utility.
record.recipe_differences: Uses target-model versus teacher-model activation differences, selects a task-specific intervention layer and strength, then adds the vector during inference. It does not use the specified harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction or ablate it.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt format and target group affect reported outcomes; the paper reports substantially different refusal effects across freeform and choice prompts and across ToxiGen groups. It selects intervention layers and strengths by search, but those selection values are not recorded as outcome rows.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a target-minus-teacher steering vector at one searched layer of Llama2-7b-Chat and Vicuna-7b-V1.5 cuts keyword-based refusal. On ToxiGen it falls 97.29→17.00 and 62.71→2.71; on AdvBench freeform 75.58→48.27 and 81.92→1.73. Effects vary by prompt format and target group. Refusal rose on Llama2 BOLD choice prompts (9.09→15.23) and barely moved on Vicuna ToxiGen choice prompts (86.14→77.86).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single additive activation vector from aligned-vs-unaligned model activation differences can suppress refusal at inference time. The size and direction of the effect depend on model, prompt format and dataset, and come with reduced output utility.

record.peer_reviewed: CIKM ’24, 33rd ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management
record.problems: No random-direction or ablation control is reported for the refusal-direction claim; the intervention is a different, task-specific vector. No uncertainty estimates are stated. The paper notes that some attack outputs may lack practical utility and does not report a general-capability check.
record.rows_left_out: TruthfulQA scores, ToxiGen toxic-generation rates, BOLD sentiment scores, and attack-baseline comparisons were left out because they do not measure a refusal outcome named by the claim versions. ToxiGen group-level refusal values and Table 1 refusal values are included.

untested.parts: No harmful-minus-harmless direction. No directional ablation. No addition to induce refusal on harmless prompts. No capability check; the authors note steered AdvBench outputs lose utility.
No weight edit or abliterated release.
No analysis of whether jailbreaks (GCG etc.) suppress the refusal direction. No adversarial training against ablation.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal.
No transfer across languages, variants or base-to-instruct models. The vector uses base/teacher activations but no transfer is tested.

record.verdict_notes: Row values match Tables 1 and 2. Table 2 is in proportions; Table 1 is in percent. Refusal is detected by keyword matching, and disclaimers like 'I'm just an AI' are not counted as refusal. The §4.4 dot-product analysis with a 'refusal vector' is qualitative, on one prompt at layer 16, and gives no rate. Table 8 compares the authors' method with baselines and is correctly left out. There are no random-vector controls and no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction; no ablation of that direction; no addition of that direction to induce refusal on harmless requests; no general-capability check.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
No test of attacks suppressing the specified refusal direction and no training against its ablation.
No comparison of a single direction with an affine, cone, or multi-direction account of refusal.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No transfer test of the specified direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
No test varying refusal-training method or timing.
